assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Simple cell
items.clue: Two different metals in contact with a conducting solution.

items.label: Non-rechargeable cell
items.clue: Stops working for good once one of its reactants is used up.

items.label: Electrolyte
items.clue: The conducting liquid or paste containing ions that can move.

items.label: Battery
items.clue: Two or more cells connected together to give a greater voltage.

questions.stem: A chemical cell is connected to a lamp and the lamp lights. Where does the electricity come from?

options.text: From chemicals inside the cell that react together
From electricity stored in the cell already
From a store of electrons in the metal casing
From energy stored inside it, like a battery

questions.explanation: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity; the reaction runs only once the circuit is complete.

questions.stem: Where does the hydrogen in a hydrogen fuel cell come from?

options.text: It is stored inside the cell when the cell is built
It is made inside the cell from air and water
It is released by the electrolyte as it runs
It is fed in from an external supply of the fuel

questions.explanation: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air.

questions.stem: Two cells are identical except that one uses zinc and copper electrodes and the other uses magnesium and copper. The cells give different voltages. Why?

options.text: The voltage depends on how much electrolyte there is
The voltage depends on the type of electrode used
The voltage depends on the area of the electrode
The voltage depends on the wire joining them up

questions.explanation: The voltage produced by a cell depends on a number of factors, including the type of electrode.

questions.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell, how does the fuel produce a potential difference?

options.text: It is oxidised electrochemically at an electrode
It is burned, and the heat drives a generator
It is reduced by oxygen at the negative electrode
It is decomposed by a current supplied to the cell

questions.explanation: The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference.

questions.stem: A simple cell uses zinc and copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by a different electrolyte, with everything else unchanged. What happens to the voltage?

options.text: It stays the same, because only the metals matter here
It stays the same for any liquid, even for pure water
It may change, as the voltage depends on electrolyte
It changes only if the new electrolyte is an acid

questions.explanation: The voltage produced by a cell depends on the type of electrolyte as well as the type of electrode.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?

options.text: H2 + O2 → H2O + O
H2 + O2 → 2H2O

questions.explanation: The overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water, balanced as 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

questions.stem: Which pair of electrodes, dipped into an electrolyte, would produce a voltage?

options.text: Two identical strips of copper metal
Two copper strips of different size
Two carbon rods taken from cells
A zinc strip and a copper strip

questions.explanation: A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte.

questions.stem: Why are hydrogen fuel cells described as a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries?

options.text: They can be refilled with electricity at any charge point
They store far more electricity inside them than a battery
They need no fuel or oxygen once they have been started
They keep working while hydrogen is supplied, with no recharging

questions.explanation: A fuel cell runs on an external fuel supply, so it does not have to be taken out of use to recharge.

questions.stem: A battery is made by connecting four 1.5 V cells together in series. What voltage does the battery provide, and why?

options.text: 1.5 V, because the cells share one voltage
6.0 V, because the voltages of the cells add up
6.0 V, because the current from each cell adds
0.375 V, as the voltage is split between them

questions.explanation: Batteries consist of two or more cells connected in series to provide a greater voltage.

questions.stem: A car maker compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a rechargeable battery car. Which is a genuine disadvantage of the fuel cell car?

options.text: It gives out carbon dioxide as it is driven
Hydrogen is difficult to store safely
It must be plugged in and recharged often
It stops once its battery has gone flat

questions.explanation: Hydrogen is a flammable gas that must be stored under pressure or at very low temperature, which is a real drawback.

questions.stem: A non-rechargeable cell stops producing a voltage after some time in use. Why does it stop?

options.text: All the electrons inside the cell have been used up
The electrolyte has leaked out of its case
One of the reactants has been completely used up
Both of the electrodes have been fully used up

questions.explanation: In non-rechargeable cells the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.

questions.stem: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?

options.text: They can be recharged from the mains many times over
They are rechargeable once the alkali is replaced
They work again once fresh reactants are added
They are non-rechargeable, so they are replaced

questions.explanation: The specification states that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.

questions.stem: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode, losing electrons: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−.

questions.stem: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode, gaining electrons: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O.
